title: Nevada Policy Research Institute v. Miller
description: Whether dual employment of state legislators in the Nevada State Assembly or Senate with state higher education institutions or local government entities violates the constitutional separation of powers.
plaintiff_argument: The Nevada Policy Research Institute (NPRI) argued that dual service by legislators in state or local government positions violates the constitutional separation of powers, as these positions are part of or exercise functions appertaining to the executive department.
defendant_argument: The respondents (legislators and the Legislature) argued that the separation of powers only applies to public officers exercising sovereign functions, not public employees, and does not bar employment with local government.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's dismissal, ruling that the dual employments of the respondent legislators with the Nevada System of Higher Education or local government entities do not violate the constitutional separation of powers.

title: Mass Land Acquisition, LLC v. The First Judicial District Court of the State
description: Whether a private utility company, delegated eminent domain power, can take private property for a natural gas pipeline as a "public use" under the Nevada Constitution, and whether a jury must determine if the taking is actually for a public use.
plaintiff_argument: Mass Land argued that NV Energy, as a private entity, cannot establish "public use" to condemn an easement across its property, violating the Nevada Constitution's prohibition against direct or indirect transfer of property from one private party to another, and that it was entitled to a jury determination on whether the taking was actually for a public use.
defendant_argument: NV Energy argued that as a regulated public utility with delegated eminent domain power, it acts as "the government" for purposes of eminent domain, and the taking for a natural gas pipeline is a statutorily recognized public use not prohibited by the Nevada Constitution's private-to-private transfer clause, which applies only to subsequent transfers. It also argued there were no genuine issues of material fact requiring a jury.
decision_outcome: The court denied Mass Land's petition for extraordinary writ relief, upholding the district court's orders that allowed NV Energy to take an easement for a natural gas pipeline and denied a jury determination on public use.

title: Fleischmann v. Aguilar
description: Whether the district court erred in denying Jennifer Fleischmann's request to prevent a voter identification ballot initiative from being placed on the ballot.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff argued that the ballot initiative should not be placed on the ballot because it includes an unfunded mandate and its description of effect is legally insufficient.
defendant_argument: The defendant argued that the ballot initiative does not include an unfunded mandate and its description of effect is legally sufficient, thus it should be placed on the ballot.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's order, denying the plaintiff's request for declaratory and injunctive relief, thereby allowing the ballot initiative to proceed.

title: Sisolak v. Polymer80
description: Whether Nevada statutes regulating unfinished firearms (ghost guns) are unconstitutionally vague.
plaintiff_argument: The statutes regulating unfinished firearms are unconstitutionally vague because their definitions are unclear and they lack a scienter requirement, leading to arbitrary enforcement.
defendant_argument: The challenged statutes are not unconstitutionally vague, provide fair notice of what is prohibited, and include a scienter requirement, thus not posing a risk of arbitrary enforcement.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's order, finding that the statutes regulating unfinished firearms are not unconstitutionally vague and their enforcement is not enjoined.

title: Nevadans For Reproductive Freedom v. Washington et al.
description: Whether an initiative petition establishing a constitutional right to reproductive freedom in Nevada meets the state's legal requirements for ballot initiatives, specifically regarding the single-subject rule, the sufficiency of its description of effect, and the requirement for revenue if it mandates expenditure.
plaintiff_argument: The initiative petition complies with the single-subject requirement, has a legally sufficient description of effect, and does not require an expenditure of money without providing a revenue source.
defendant_argument: The initiative petition violates Nevada's single-subject requirement, its description of effect is misleading and fails to provide essential information, and it requires an expenditure of money without providing the necessary funding.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's order, thereby allowing the initiative petition to be placed on the 2024 ballot.

title: I.S. v. State
description: Whether NRS 62C.200(1)(b)'s requirement for prosecutorial consent before a juvenile court can dismiss a petition and refer a juvenile to informal supervision violates the separation of powers doctrine.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, I.S., argued that the prosecutorial consent requirement unconstitutionally infringes on the juvenile court's sentencing discretion, thereby violating the separation of powers between the executive and judicial branches.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Nevada, argued that the statute does not create a separation of powers issue because the juvenile court's authority is statutory, not constitutional, and the dismissal/referral to informal supervision is not a sentencing decision.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the district court's order, concluding that the prosecutorial-consent requirement for informal supervision does not violate the separation of powers doctrine.

title: Valley Health System v. Murray
description: Whether both the governor and the chief justice have the authority to designate temporary substitutes for disqualified justices on the supreme court, or if only the governor has this authority.
plaintiff_argument: Centennial Hills argued that the Nevada Constitution, article 6, section 4(2), bestows upon the governor sole authority to designate substitute justices in cases of disqualification, and those substitutes must be sitting lower court judges.
defendant_argument: Dwayne Anthony Murray argued that the chief justice's authority to temporarily assign senior justices under article 6, section 19(1), is concurrent, complementary, and compatible with the governor's authority under section 4(2).
decision_outcome: The court overruled Centennial Hills' objection and denied its motion to designate replacement justices, concluding that the chief justice's assignment of senior justices was constitutionally authorized.

title: Mack v. Williams
description: Whether a private right of action for retrospective monetary relief exists under Article 1, Section 18 of the Nevada Constitution for violations of search-and-seizure rights, and whether state-actor defendants can raise qualified immunity as a defense to such actions.
plaintiff_argument: Mack argued that the Nevada Constitution's Article 1, Section 18, establishes an implied private right of action for monetary relief for search-and-seizure violations, and that qualified immunity, being a federal doctrine, does not apply as a defense to state constitutional claims.
defendant_argument: The NDOC parties contended that no private right of action for monetary relief exists under the Nevada Constitution or authorized by the Legislature, and if such a right were recognized, qualified immunity should apply as a defense.
decision_outcome: The court ruled that a private right of action for retrospective monetary relief exists under Article 1, Section 18 of the Nevada Constitution for violations of search-and-seizure rights, and that qualified immunity is not an available defense for state actors in such actions.

title: ACLU of Nevada v. The County of Nye
description: Whether Nye County's proposed election procedures, including livestreaming hand-counts, limiting ADA touchscreen use, and requiring specific identification for signature verification, comply with state and federal election laws.
plaintiff_argument: The petitioners argued that Nye County's proposed procedures for orally announcing ballot selections during hand-counts, limiting touchscreen use to those with 'special needs,' and requiring identification for signature verification violate constitutional, statutory, and federal election laws.
defendant_argument: The respondents contended that the presentation of election procedures was a general overview and that the petitioners were speculating and distorting information to allege nonexistent election law violations.
decision_outcome: The court granted in part the petition for a writ of mandamus, ordering Nye County to cease livestreaming vote counts before polls close, ensure observers do not prematurely release results, and provide all statutory methods for voter identity verification; the court denied the petition regarding the ADA touchscreen issue.

title: Education Freedom PAC v. Reid
description: Whether an initiative petition proposing a constitutional amendment for education freedom accounts is valid under Nevada constitutional and statutory requirements, specifically regarding funding provisions, description of effect, and legislative deliberative functions.
plaintiff_argument: The initiative did not need to comply with the unfunded mandate requirement because it proposed a constitutional change, not a statutory one, and its description of effect was adequate and did not impede the Legislature's deliberative function.
defendant_argument: The initiative is invalid because it is an unfunded mandate, its description of effect is legally misleading, and it violates the Nevada Legislature's inherent deliberative functions.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Nevada affirmed the district court's order, enjoining the circulation of the initiative petition and its placement on the ballot, declaring the initiative void.

title: Cegavske v. Hollowood
description: Whether NRS 295.026, which allows initiative petition sponsors to withdraw their petitions, is constitutional, thereby nullifying the Secretary of State's duty to place them on the ballot, or if the Secretary has a constitutional duty to place all verified petitions on the ballot regardless of withdrawal.
plaintiff_argument: The Secretary of State argued that NRS 295.026 is unconstitutional because it infringes on public rights vested by the initiative-petition process and conflicts with her constitutional duty to place verified initiative petitions on the ballot if the Legislature does not act.
defendant_argument: The sponsors argued that NRS 295.026 is a permissible exercise of the Legislature's power to enact statutes facilitating the people's initiative power, and that a withdrawn petition is void, nullifying the Secretary's duty to place it on the ballot.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed in part, ruling that NRS 295.026 is constitutional and that withdrawn initiative petitions are void, thus compelling the Secretary of State not to place them on the ballot. It reversed in part, finding that a writ of prohibition was not appropriate for the Secretary's ministerial action.

title: Shea v. State
description: Whether the adequacy of Nevada's public education system, including its funding and quality, is a justiciable issue for the courts or a nonjusticiable political question textually committed to the Legislature.
plaintiff_argument: Shea argued that Nevada's public education system fails its students due to inadequate funding and resources, violating the Nevada Constitution's education clauses, and sought judicial intervention to declare a basic right to sufficient education and enjoin inadequate funding systems.
defendant_argument: The State argued that Shea's claims present nonjusticiable political questions because the Nevada Constitution textually commits education policy, including funding, to the broad discretion of the Legislature, and courts lack judicially manageable standards to resolve such issues.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Nevada affirmed the district court's dismissal of the complaint, concluding that the claims regarding the adequacy of public education are nonjusticiable political questions.

title: Caruso v. Eighth Judicial District Court of Nevada
description: Whether a legislator's dual service as a prosecutor violates the separation of powers doctrine, with the plaintiff arguing it does and warrants dismissal of charges, and the defendant arguing dismissal is not the correct remedy and the court should not address the constitutional issue if not necessary.
plaintiff_argument: The plaintiff, Samuel Caruso, argued that Deputy District Attorney Melanie Scheible's dual service as a prosecutor and legislator violated the separation of powers doctrine, and therefore, the criminal charges against him should be dismissed.
defendant_argument: The defendant, the State of Nevada, argued that dismissal of the criminal charges was not the appropriate remedy for the alleged separation-of-powers violation, and that the court should avoid ruling on constitutional questions if not absolutely necessary to resolve the case.
decision_outcome: The court denied the petition for a writ of mandamus, concluding that the petitioner had not demonstrated that dismissal of the criminal charges was an available remedy, and thus extraordinary relief was not warranted.

title: Aguirre v. Elko County Sheriff's Office
description: Whether Nevada's homestead exemption protects real property from civil forfeiture, and whether an incarcerated individual can qualify as a bona fide resident for homestead exemption purposes.
plaintiff_argument: The homestead exemption protects his property from civil forfeiture, and his incarceration is a temporary absence that does not negate his bona fide residency for homestead purposes.
defendant_argument: Public policy warrants a forfeiture exception for property used in drug offenses, and an incarcerated individual cannot satisfy the residency requirement for a homestead exemption.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's judgment of forfeiture, ruling that the homestead exemption protects the property from civil forfeiture and that Aguirre qualified for the exemption.

title: Nevada Policy Research Institute, Inc. v. Cannizzaro
description: Whether the public-importance exception to standing applies to a case challenging the dual service of state legislators as state or local government employees, even when the challenge does not involve a legislative expenditure or appropriation.
plaintiff_argument: NPRI argued that the dual service of legislators as state/local government employees violates the Nevada Constitution's separation-of-powers clause and that it has standing under the public-importance exception, which should be expanded to cover such constitutional challenges.
defendant_argument: The defendants argued that NPRI lacked traditional standing due to no personal injury and did not meet the public-importance exception because the case did not challenge a specific legislative expenditure or appropriation, nor was NPRI the sole appropriate party.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's dismissal, expanding the public-importance exception to grant standing to NPRI for its separation-of-powers challenge, and remanded the case for further proceedings.

title: Aparicio v. State
description: Whether the district court erred by broadly interpreting the definition of "victim" under Marsy's Law and NRS 176.015 to include anyone impacted by a crime, thereby improperly considering victim impact statements from non-victims during sentencing, with the plaintiff arguing this was an abuse of discretion and the defendant arguing the statements were properly considered or any error was harmless.
plaintiff_argument: Aparicio argued that the district court abused its discretion by admitting and relying on dozens of improper victim impact letters from individuals who did not qualify as "victims" under Nevada law, warranting a new sentencing hearing.
defendant_argument: The State argued that the district court properly considered the impact statements because their authors were legitimate victims under Nevada law, and even if there was an error, it was harmless.
decision_outcome: The court affirmed the judgment of conviction but vacated the sentence and remanded the case for resentencing before a different district court judge.

title: Myers  v. Reno Cab Co.
description: Whether taxicab drivers are "employees" or "independent contractors" for purposes of minimum wage and waiting time penalties, and whether contractual recitations or Nevada Transportation Authority (NTA) approval are conclusive in determining this status.
plaintiff_argument: The drivers argue they are employees under the "economic realities" test for Minimum Wage Amendment (MWA) claims and are entitled to waiting time penalties under NRS 608.040, regardless of contractual disavowals or NTA lease approvals.
defendant_argument: The cab companies argue the drivers are independent contractors based on contractual recitations and the NTA's approval of their leases, which they claim forecloses further inquiry into employee status for all purposes.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment in favor of the cab companies and remanded the case for further proceedings, holding that contractual recitations and NTA lease approvals are not conclusive in determining employee status for minimum wage and waiting time penalty claims.

title: Ortiz v. State
description: Whether a prosecutor's argument that a defendant tailored his trial testimony to the evidence violates the defendant's constitutional right to be present at trial.
plaintiff_argument: Ortiz argued the district court erred by failing to conduct an evidentiary hearing on the jury venire, allowing the prosecutor to argue he tailored his testimony, and improperly instructing the jury on sexual assault.
defendant_argument: The State argued the district court properly denied the evidentiary hearing, the prosecutor's tailoring argument was permissible and did not violate Ortiz's rights, and the jury instructions were accurate.
decision_outcome: The Supreme Court of Nevada affirmed the judgment of conviction.

title: Doe v. La Fuente, Inc.
description: Whether exotic dancers are employees entitled to minimum wage protections under the Nevada Minimum Wage Amendment (MWA), or independent contractors as defined by NRS 608.0155.
plaintiff_argument: The Doe Dancers argued they are employees under the MWA's constitutional protections, applying the economic realities test, and that NRS 608.0155 cannot abrogate these constitutional rights.
defendant_argument: La Fuente (Cheetahs) argued that NRS 608.0155, which conclusively presumes certain workers to be independent contractors, applies to MWA claims, thus making the dancers ineligible for minimum wages.
decision_outcome: The court reversed the district court's summary judgment, holding that the economic realities test applies to MWA claims, the Doe Dancers are employees under that test, and NRS 608.0155 does not abrogate their constitutional minimum wage protections.
